strengths: LPAM addresses a practical failure of image stitching: seam selection cannot repair residual geometric misalignment. Its training-free, localized refinement offers a useful way to improve existing pipelines without redesigning their initial alignment methods.

Tables 1–2 report consistent average improvements across 79 image pairs, three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five alignment methods. For example, adding LPAM to the REW-based baseline improves SEAGULL SSIM from 0.638 to 0.697. This breadth supports the module’s practical applicability.

The pipeline is understandable, with helpful diagrams and pseudocode. Local flow attenuation and constrained seam reconnection have clear motivations, and Figures 1 and 7 show visible repairs to structural discontinuities.
The parameter ablations and explicit failure analysis provide useful insight into the alignment–smoothness tradeoff. Core methods and existing datasets are attributed, and a code URL is provided.
weaknesses: The main evidence gap concerns final mosaic quality. All four quantitative metrics measure inter-image agreement around the selected seam, leaving distortions and artifacts elsewhere insufficiently assessed. Table 3 demonstrates this mismatch: removing flow attenuation improves Parallax SSIM from 0.782 to 0.819, although Figure 3 shows resulting artifacts. Broader perceptual or geometric evaluation, including the frequency of degradation across image pairs, is needed to substantiate the overall quality claim.

Originality is primarily in the localized, modular combination of established techniques. The distinction from seam-guided local alignment [22] and dense-matching-based seam estimation [35] needs sharper treatment; the description of previous methods as operating on settled pre-aligned images is too broad even relative to the paper’s own related-work discussion. Quantitative comparisons with these closely related approaches, or a simpler dense-refinement baseline, would better establish the contribution beyond adding alignment capacity.

The claim of dissociating seam quality from initial alignment is stronger than the algorithm supports. In Section 3.2, max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) can classify a uniformly high-error seam as plausible and skip refinement entirely. This is relevant to poor initial alignment, yet the paper provides neither an absolute quality safeguard nor controlled experiments characterizing this failure.

The smooth-reinsertion argument remains heuristic. The one-dimensional sigmoid in Section 3.3 does not establish continuity around the complete rectangular patch boundary, while fixing seam labels establishes label compatibility rather than pixel continuity. The acknowledged small-patch failure makes explicit boundary handling and systematic assessment of newly introduced artifacts particularly important.

Efficiency and reproducibility need fuller reporting. Section 4.4 records LPAM separately, so its roughly 6–10 seconds are additional to host seam-cutting times, which are often comparable or smaller. Image resolutions and end-to-end comparisons are needed to assess the lightweight claim. Alignment-patch padding, orientation and overlap handling, SIFT-flow settings, and acquisition/preprocessing details for the new dataset are also insufficiently specified in the supplied manuscript.
